findings.title: Removed or downgraded users keep access via refresh-token re-issue
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:230 (POST /api/v1/auth/refreshToken; whitelisted in packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:27, so it bypasses the global API-key/JWT gate in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285).
Attacker: an authenticated member who has been removed from a workspace/organization, deactivated, or had their role downgraded, crossing the revocation boundary — they keep obtaining fresh, fully privileged credentials.
Path: the handler reads only the refresh-token cookie (line 231) and verifies its signature (line 234); the decrypted payload/meta is used solely for a null check (line 251) and is never compared with the caller, so the refresh credential is not bound to any subject. The identity used to mint the new credentials is taken verbatim from req.user (line 237), i.e. the passport session blob, and passed to setTokenOrCookies (lines 260 and 262), which signs a new auth token carrying that user's cached activeWorkspaceId, permissions and isOrganizationAdmin (lines 304, 393-402). Nothing on the path re-reads the user, workspace-user or organization-user rows, and passport.deserializeUser (lines 93-95) returns the stored object unchanged.
Why nothing stops it: workspace/organization membership removal, user deactivation and role changes never touch the session store — destroyAllSessionsForUser is only called from password-change paths (packages/server/src/enterprise/services/user.service.ts:185 and account.service.ts:601) — and this endpoint happily re-issues credentials from the surviving session, with each refresh also touching/extending the session. The refresh token itself lives 90 days (JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRY_IN_MINUTES default, line 388).
Impact: revocation is ineffective for the life of the session; a removed member or downgraded user keeps API access with the old permissions and can keep renewing it indefinitely, and any party holding a valid refresh token plus any live session receives tokens for that session's user because the token's id/meta is never checked against the session.
Fix: in the refresh handler, reload the user, workspace-user and organization-user records from the database, reject the refresh if the workspace membership no longer exists, the status is not ACTIVE, or the role changed, and compare the refresh token's decrypted meta id with the session user's id before minting. Also invalidate sessions and revoke refresh tokens when a member is removed, deactivated or has a role changed.

findings.title: Authenticated user can reach org-wide BullMQ dashboard and mutate other tenants' jobs
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/index.ts:335 (`this.app.use('/admin/queues', rateLimiter, verifyTokenForBullMQDashboard, this.queueManager.getBullBoardRouter())`).
Attacker: any authenticated workspace user with any role (for example a viewer with no administrative permission), crossing from their own tenant into org-wide/cross-tenant queue administration.
Path: the only guard on the BullBoard UI is verifyTokenForBullMQDashboard, which calls passport.authenticate('jwt') and then checks only err/info/user and license validity (lines 433-457); it never inspects isOrganizationAdmin, permissions or any admin permission, unlike the enterprise routes that use checkPermission/checkAnyPermission (packages/server/src/enterprise/rbac/PermissionCheck.ts). The handler then hands the request to this.queueManager.getBullBoardRouter() (packages/server/src/queue/QueueManager.ts:100-103, 158-162), the raw @bull-board express adapter over every registered queue.
Why nothing stops it: the middleware returns next() for any caller who merely has a valid session/JWT, so a low-privileged user reaches a surface that lists jobs and payloads from all workspaces and offers retry/promote/clean/remove actions on them; no route-level permission decorator exists on this mount, and BullBoard itself performs no authorization.
Impact: in a multi-tenant/enterprise deployment with the dashboard enabled, a normal workspace user can read job data (including prediction inputs/outputs) belonging to other workspaces and can mutate or delete other tenants' jobs — a horizontal and vertical privilege escalation.
Fix: gate /admin/queues with an organization-admin check (e.g. require req.user.isOrganizationAdmin or a dedicated admin permission via checkAnyPermission) in addition to verifyTokenForBullMQDashboard, or disable the dashboard whenever the platform is not single-tenant.

findings.title: Default JWT secrets let anyone forge refresh tokens and mint access tokens
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:230 (app.post('/api/v1/auth/refreshToken'), registered from initializeJwtCookieMiddleware, which index.ts:213 runs before the global API-key/JWT gate at index.ts:215, so the route is reachable with no session, no API key and no token).
Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller, crossing the boundary that separates an anonymous request from the server's own authentication tokens.
Path: req.cookies.refreshToken (line 231) -> jwt.verify(refreshToken, jwtRefreshSecret, ...) (line 234) -> decryptToken(payload.meta) (line 251) -> setTokenOrCookies(res, loggedInUser, false, req) (line 262) -> res.cookie('token', generateJwtAuthToken(...)) (lines 338-342), where the access token is signed with jwtAuthTokenSecret.
Why nothing on the path stops it: jwtRefreshSecret is not configuration that the deployment must supply; it falls back to the literal 'refresh_token' (line 34, itself falling back to JWT_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET), so any deployment that does not set JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_SECRET/JWT_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET verifies against a value printed in this source file. jsonwebtoken accepts HS256 with a string secret, so the attacker signs {id, username, meta} with 'refresh_token' and the verify at line 234 succeeds. The only further check is that decryptToken(payload.meta) returns something, and that key also defaults to the literal 'Secre$t' (tempTokenUtils.ts:33/52), so the attacker supplies any meta it wants. The handler never binds the token to the caller's own identity; it takes identity from req.user and then mints a new access-token cookie with the other literal secret ('auth_token', line 33).
Impact: on a default deployment the refresh endpoint accepts tokens minted offline by anyone who read this file and answers by issuing a freshly signed access-token cookie; the same literal key signs the tokens that guard every /api/v1 route (jwtOptions.secretOrKey, line 47), so the application has no secret protecting the credentials it issues and accepts.
Fix: require JWT_REFRESH_TOKEN_SECRET and JWT_AUTH_TOKEN_SECRET explicitly and fail closed at startup if they are missing or shorter than a strong random value; pass algorithms: ['HS256'] to jwt.verify; compare the decrypted meta against the authenticated session user before issuing anything.

findings.title: Session cookie forged via hard-coded default secret 'flowise'
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:80 (app.use(session(options)) built from _initializePassportMiddleware, line 52-63), whose options are consumed by passport.session() (line 82) and by the JWT strategy that reads req.user (AuthStrategy.ts:25-38).
Attacker: any caller able to reach the app over HTTP, crossing the boundary between an anonymous request and the server-side session that supplies the authenticated user object.
Path: the session cookie is the only thing that carries the session id, and passport.serializeUser/deserializeUser (lines 89-95) store and return the whole LoggedInUser verbatim, so req.user - the identity the JWT strategy compares against the token's meta (AuthStrategy.ts:35) - is exactly the object held in that session. The cookie is signed with secret: process.env.EXPRESS_SESSION_SECRET || 'flowise' (line 55).
Why nothing on the path stops it: the signing key is a literal shipped in the repository, and no code checks that EXPRESS_SESSION_SECRET was configured, so on any deployment that does not set it the key that gives the session cookie its integrity is known to anyone who reads this file; combined with the defaulted JWT keys above, both halves of the session+token scheme are protected by published values.
Impact: the integrity of the session cookie - the sole source of req.user, and therefore of every authorization decision made downstream of this middleware (including isOrganizationAdmin/permissions/activeWorkspaceId carried in the session object) - rests on a key that is not secret, and sessions cannot be cryptographically distinguished from attacker-crafted ones once a valid session id is in play.
Fix: require EXPRESS_SESSION_SECRET with no default and fail closed at startup when it is missing, and store only an opaque user id in the session so the authoritative user record is re-read from the database on each request.

findings.title: Deactivated workspace user can log in and is silently reactivated with full access
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:267 (POST /api/v1/auth/login, unauthenticated and whitelisted in packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:26) reaching the local strategy at index.ts:111. Attacker: a user whose workspace/organization access an administrator has disabled (WorkspaceUserStatus.DISABLE / a suspended OrganizationUser row) - crossing the admin's access-revocation boundary. Path: the login strategy calls accountService.login (account.service.ts:450-505), which looks the user up by email and only checks the password hash (compareHash, line 469) and the User row's UNVERIFIED status; it then resolves the caller's membership through readWorkspaceUserByLastLogin (workspace-user.service.ts:188-209), a query filtered on userId and lastLogin only - there is no status predicate anywhere in it. Back in the strategy, lines 129-142 unconditionally overwrite workspaceUser.status = WorkspaceUserStatus.ACTIVE and organizationUser.status = OrganizationUserStatus.ACTIVE and persist both records with updateWorkspaceUser/updateOrganizationUser before returning the fully privileged LoggedInUser (permissions parsed from the role at line 182, isOrganizationAdmin at line 178). Nothing on the path stops this: a repo-wide search shows WorkspaceUserStatus.DISABLE ('disable', workspace-user.entity.ts:8) is never compared to anything in the server, so the disabled flag is never enforced at login, and the login handler itself is the code that clears it. Impact: deactivating or suspending a member of a workspace/organization - the intended offboarding control - is silently undone by the very next login of that user; a removed or suspended user keeps full workspace access, keeps their role permissions, and their membership rows are rewritten as active, so the admin's revocation appears to have been reverted. Fix: reject the login when the resolved WorkspaceUser status is DISABLE (or the OrganizationUser status is not ACTIVE) before building LoggedInUser, and only set these statuses to ACTIVE from the invite-acceptance/verification flow, never from a plain password login.

findings.title: Session and auth cookies issued without Secure flag, enabling session hijack over HTTP
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:58-62 (session cookie options), with the same value used for the auth cookies in setTokenOrCookies at lines 325-334 and 338-347.
Attacker: a network attacker on the path between the browser and the server, or anyone able to make the browser issue a plain http:// request to the app's host — crossing from no credentials into the victim's session.
Path: lines 38-45 compute secureCookie, which is false unless SECURE_COOKIES==='true' or APP_URL starts with 'https'; line 59 passes it as `secure: secureCookie` for the session cookie and lines 327/332/341/346 for the `token` and `refreshToken` cookies. A deployment served over HTTPS by a reverse proxy/load balancer but with APP_URL unset (the shipped packages/server/.env.example leaves APP_URL commented out at line 84) therefore issues connect.sid, token and refreshToken without the Secure attribute.
Why nothing stops it: the browser sends non-Secure cookies on any plaintext request to the same host and the server accepts them unchanged; httpOnly only blocks JavaScript, and SameSite=lax does not prevent cleartext transmission of a same-site http request.
Impact: the session cookie carries the whole LoggedInUser and the refresh cookie is valid for 90 days by default, so one http:// request to the app's host — a user typing the hostname, an http link, a downgraded subresource, or an active MITM — hands the attacker a replayable credential for full account access; an active attacker can also overwrite these cookies over http.
Fix: default `secure: true` and require an explicit opt-out (SECURE_COOKIES=false) for genuinely plaintext setups, require APP_URL to be set, and consider `__Host-` prefixed cookie names.

findings.title: Cross-site login POST silently logs victim into attacker's Flowise account
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:267 (POST /api/v1/auth/login; session established at lines 277-287).
Attacker: any website the victim visits — an unauthenticated cross-site attacker — crossing into the victim's browser, which ends up logged into the attacker's Flowise account without the victim's knowledge.
Path: `/api/v1/auth/login` is in WHITELIST_URLS (utils/constants.ts:26), so index.ts:221-225 lets the request through with no session, no API key and without the custom `x-request-from: internal` header that non-whitelisted /api/v1 routes require (index.ts:224); the handler authenticates with the body's email/password (lines 105-111), regenerates the session (line 277), calls req.login (line 282) and setTokenOrCookies writes the token/refreshToken cookies (line 286). No CSRF token or Origin/Referer check exists anywhere in packages/server/src (no csrf/csurf middleware), and express.urlencoded is enabled (index.ts:159), so a cross-site `<form method=POST>` carrying the attacker's credentials is enough.
Why nothing stops it: the app's only CSRF-style defense is the custom `x-request-from: internal` header enforced for non-whitelisted paths, and this route is whitelisted; SameSite=lax on the response cookies does not stop the browser from storing cookies set by a cross-site form POST (form submissions are top-level navigations).
Impact: the victim continues working in what looks like their own session while every secret they enter (model/API keys in credentials, uploaded documents, chatflows, agent tools) is stored in the attacker's account/workspace, which the attacker can log into and read afterwards; flows in that workspace (custom code/tool nodes, prompts) are also executed under the victim's deployment.
Fix: require a CSRF token (synchronizer or double-submit) or at minimum validate Origin/Referer on the auth POST routes, and set SameSite=Strict for the auth cookies.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /auth/resolve leaks DB connections, exhausting the pool
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:195 (app.post('/api/v1/auth/resolve', ...), registered before the global /api/v1 auth middleware in index.ts:215, so it is reachable unauthenticated).
Attacker: any unauthenticated network caller, crossing the boundary of fair use of the server's DB connection pool: a request whose DB work fails leaves a dedicated pooled connection checked out forever.
Path: line 204 const queryRunner = expressApp.AppDataSource.createQueryRunner(); line 205 await queryRunner.connect(); line 206 await orgService.countOrganizations(queryRunner); line 207 await queryRunner.release(). The release at line 207 is reached only if countOrganizations resolves: there is no try/finally, so any rejection from connect()/count() (DB error, statement timeout, or pool saturation produced by a concurrent flood of this same unauthenticated route) skips the release and the connection is never returned to the pool. The async route handler also has no try/catch, so the rejection itself escapes the handler.
Nothing on the path stops this: there is no auth check, no rate limit and no error handling around the query runner on this route, and it is deliberately outside the global auth middleware. Other services in the same codebase (e.g. account.service.ts:442) release query runners in finally, so the omission here is an oversight, not a deliberate lifecycle.
Impact: TypeORM's pool is small by default (~10 connections); a handful of failed requests during any DB hiccup (which the flood itself can provoke) permanently removes connections from the pool and cascades into every DB-backed endpoint on the instance failing, turning a transient error into a persistent outage; the unhandled rejection can additionally terminate the process depending on process-level handlers.
Fix: wrap the connect/count in try { ... } finally { if (queryRunner && !queryRunner.isReleased) await queryRunner.release() } so the connection is returned on every path, and reject early if connect() fails.

findings.title: Authenticated SSO user exhausts server heap with unbounded in-memory SSO token cache
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/middleware/passport/index.ts:319 storeSSOUserPayload(ssoToken, returnUser) inside setTokenOrCookies when redirect=true, reached from every SSO callback route (GoogleSSO.ts:108, AzureSSO.ts:59, Auth0SSO.ts:103, GithubSSO.ts:92).
Attacker: an authenticated user who can complete an SSO login against the configured identity provider (for example any employee with a Google/Azure account in an SSO-enabled deployment), crossing the boundary from consuming their own per-login resources to permanently consuming server-global memory they cannot be charged for.
Path: SSO callback -> req.login -> setTokenOrCookies(..., redirect=true) -> line 462 app.cachePool.addSSOTokenCache(ssoToken, returnUser) -> CachePool.ts:51-59, where in the default (non-queue) mode line 58 executes this.ssoTokenCache[ssoToken] = value. The key is a fresh uuidv4 per login, so every login adds a new entry containing the full serialized LoggedInUser (permissions, features, assignedWorkspaces); entries are removed only when the browser redeems the token via the auth controller (getSSOTokenCache/deleteSSOTokenCache), which a scripted client simply never does.
Nothing on the path stops it: the in-memory branch has no TTL, no max size and no eviction, in contrast to the Redis branch at CachePool.ts:55 which explicitly sets EX 120 — the 120-second expiry is silently dropped in the default mode, so a user repeatedly triggering the SSO callback accumulates entries for the lifetime of the process with no cap; no authentication or rate limit beyond the IdP login itself bounds the loop.
Impact: unbounded growth of the Node.js heap, ending in OOM / process restart and a denial of service for all tenants of the instance; the entries are never reclaimed even after the user logs out.
Fix: give the in-memory cache the same expiry as the Redis path (store an expiry timestamp with each entry and sweep/delete expired entries, or use a bounded LRU/map with a maximum size and delete the entry when redeemed), and cap the number of outstanding SSO tokens per user.

findings.title: Unauthenticated token refresh leaks and rotates any tenant's OAuth tokens
findings.description: Entry: POST /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId (packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:307). Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller (or any API-key holder with zero permissions) who knows a credential UUID, crossing the authentication boundary and the workspace/tenant boundary into another tenant's stored OAuth credential. The value enters at req.params.credentialId (line 309), is passed straight into credentialRepository.findOneBy({ id: credentialId }) (lines 314-316) with no workspaceId and no req.user check, the decrypted credential's clientSecret and refresh_token are sent to the provider (lines 325-360), and the full provider response is echoed back as tokenInfo: { ...tokenData } (lines 393-401). Nothing stops it: /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh is in WHITELIST_URLS (packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:40), so the global middleware takes the isWhitelisted branch and calls next() without authenticating or setting req.user (packages/server/src/index.ts:221-223); the handler itself never consults req.user.activeWorkspaceId, never calls checkPermission('credentials:update'), and does not join against WorkspaceShared, unlike the credentials routes (packages/server/src/routes/credentials/index.ts:14) and services/credentials/index.ts:127-133 which scope by workspaceId. Impact: any caller who learns a credential UUID (leaked in flow configs, exports, logs or shared items) receives a freshly minted access_token and rotated refresh_token for that credential's third-party account (e.g. Microsoft Graph mailbox/OneDrive), and the server writes the rotated tokens back into the victim's credential (lines 387-390), so the attacker gains standing access to the victim's connected account while disrupting the victim's own token. Fix: remove '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh' from WHITELIST_URLS so the route requires authentication, add checkPermission('credentials:update'), look the credential up with { id, workspaceId: req.user.activeWorkspaceId } plus the shared-credential check, and never return token data in the HTTP response.

findings.title: Any authenticated caller can read another tenant's OAuth credential
findings.description: Entry: POST /api/v1/oauth2-credential/authorize/:credentialId (packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:72). Attacker: any authenticated caller, including an API key with no permissions or a user in a different workspace/tenant, crossing the tenant boundary to read another tenant's OAuth credential configuration. The value enters at req.params.credentialId (line 74) and is loaded by credentialRepository.findOneBy({ id: credentialId }) (lines 80-82) with no workspace filter; the handler then decrypts the credential (line 92) and returns the derived clientId, authorization URL, redirect URI and scope to the caller (lines 139-145). Nothing stops it: the route has no checkPermission and never reads req.user, while every sibling credentials route enforces checkPermission('credentials:view') and services/credentials.getCredentialById filters by workspaceId (packages/server/src/services/credentials/index.ts:127-133); Credential.workspaceId (packages/server/src/database/entities/Credential.ts:28) is ignored here. Impact: cross-tenant disclosure of OAuth client configuration and the ability to start an authorization flow for any tenant's credential (the returned URL carries state=<credentialId>, which is what the public callback trusts), enabling the callback-poisoning attack below. Fix: add checkPermission('credentials:view') and scope the lookup to req.user.activeWorkspaceId (with the WorkspaceShared check) before decrypting or returning any credential data.

findings.title: Attacker can overwrite another tenant's OAuth tokens via unsigned state
findings.description: Entry: GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback (packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157). Attacker: an authenticated low-privileged user in any workspace (the callback itself is unauthenticated and whitelisted) crossing the tenant boundary to overwrite another tenant's stored OAuth tokens. The value enters as req.query.state (line 159), is used verbatim as the credential id in findOneBy({ id: state }) (lines 183-185), and the client-supplied code (line 159) is exchanged with the victim credential's client_id/client_secret (lines 228-245); the provider's token response is then merged over the victim's decrypted data (lines 250-265) and written back with credentialRepository.update(credential.id, ...) (lines 271-274) with no check that the caller owns or initiated a flow for that credential. Nothing stops it: the callback is whitelisted (packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:39), the 'state' value is just the credential UUID that any authenticated caller can obtain from the authorize endpoint above, it is not signed, not single-use, and not bound to a session, user or workspace, so there is no CSRF/flow-integrity control on the write. Impact: an attacker can run the authorization URL for a victim's credential, consent at the provider with the attacker's own identity, and the server stores tokens belonging to the attacker in the victim's credential; the victim's chatflows then operate on the attacker-controlled account (data injection/exfiltration) and the victim's original refresh token is replaced, causing loss of access. Fix: issue a signed, single-use, expiring state that binds the flow to the authenticated user/workspace that started it (persisted server-side) and reject the callback unless it matches before exchanging the code or updating the credential; require the initiating user to be authorized for that credential's workspace.

findings.title: Authenticated user can make the server POST to internal URLs (SSRF via OAuth token URL)
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback), with the URL planted through packages/server/src/routes/credentials/index.ts:7 (POST /api/v1/credentials).
Attacker: a low-privileged authenticated user who can create a credential (and anyone who obtains such a credential ID) making the Flowise server issue an HTTP request to an arbitrary internal URL, crossing from "user-controlled configuration data" to "server's internal network position".
Path: the attacker POSTs /api/v1/credentials with plainDataObj {clientId, clientSecret, accessTokenUrl: 'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/'}; transformToCredentialEntity (packages/server/src/utils/index.ts:1672-1680) encrypts that object verbatim and saves it; the attacker then requests GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback?code=x&state=<credentialId>. The route is in WHITELIST_URLS (packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:39), so the global middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts:221-223 calls next() without any auth; the handler looks the credential up by the caller-supplied state with no workspace/ownership check (line 183), decrypts it, and passes accessTokenUrl straight into axios.post at line 240.
Why nothing stops it: there is no URL validation, no scheme/host allow-list, no loopback/link-local/RFC1918/metadata-address block anywhere in the server source (grep for SSRF guards returns nothing), axios follows redirects by default, and neither the callback route nor the credential lookup verifies the caller owns the credential. The only requirement is knowing a credential ID, which the attacker has for their own credential.
Impact: the Flowise server can be driven to POST to internal-only services and cloud metadata endpoints, and the fetched body is exfiltrated: for 2xx JSON responses the whole body is merged into the credential (lines 250-254) and can be read back decrypted via GET /api/v1/credentials/:id (packages/server/src/services/credentials/index.ts:143-147), and for error responses the provider body fields are rendered into the returned HTML page (lines 285-288).
Fix: validate tokenUrl before the request against an allow-list of known OAuth hosts, resolve and reject loopback, private, link-local and metadata addresses, disable redirects, and require authentication plus a workspace ownership check on the callback (state must be bound to the authenticated user).

findings.title: Unauthenticated SSRF via OAuth2 refresh credential endpoint
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:307 (POST /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId), with the URL planted through packages/server/src/routes/credentials/index.ts:7.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller who knows (or supplies) a credential ID whose stored data points accessTokenUrl at an internal address; the attacker plants the URL with a credential they created (authenticated, credentials:create) and then triggers it without any credentials, crossing into the server's internal network.
Path: the credential is stored with accessTokenUrl, clientId, clientSecret and refresh_token; the attacker calls POST /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/<credentialId>. The whitelist check uses req.path.startsWith (packages/server/src/index.ts:221) against '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh' (packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:40), so the parameterized path is also treated as whitelisted and reaches the handler with no auth; the handler reads the credential by path parameter (line 314), decrypts it, takes accessTokenUrl as tokenUrl (lines 327, 336) and calls axios.post(tokenUrl, ...) at line 355.
Why nothing stops it: the route has no authentication, no ownership check, no URL validation and no private-address/redirect protection, and the caller-supplied credentialId is used directly in findOneBy.
Impact: this is a full read SSRF primitive - the fetched response is returned to the unauthenticated caller inside tokenInfo (lines 397-401), so any JSON body from an internal service or cloud metadata endpoint is disclosed directly, and the access/refresh tokens the request generates are disclosed with it.
Fix: authenticate and authorize the refresh route (and bind it to the credential's workspace), validate tokenUrl with the same allow-list/private-IP blocking used for outbound provider calls, and stop returning raw token endpoint data to the caller.

findings.title: Reflected XSS via OAuth2 callback error params enables account takeover
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback), query parameters read at line 159. Attacker: any unauthenticated outsider who can get a victim to open a crafted link, crossing from the public internet into script execution in the victim's browser on the Flowise origin. Path: req.query.error and req.query.error_description are passed unmodified into generateErrorPage (index.ts:162-166, and the state value at line 189), which builds the page by string interpolation in generateOAuth2ResponsePage: '
${message}
' and '
${details}
' (lines 69-70) and JSON.stringify(postMessageData) inside an inline

findings.title: Reflected XSS via unescaped OAuth2 provider error in callback page
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback) reached with a state pointing at an attacker-created credential whose accessTokenUrl is a server the attacker controls. Attacker: an authenticated credential creator (credentials:create) who lures any victim into opening /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback?code=x&state=, crossing from attacker-controlled remote content into script execution in the victim's browser on the Flowise origin. Path: the callback decrypts the attacker's credential and POSTs the code to the attacker's token endpoint (line 240); the attacker's server answers 400 with {"error": "x", "error_description": ""}. The axios error is caught at line 282 and axiosError.response.data.error and error_description are interpolated into generateErrorPage (lines 285-288), which writes them raw into the HTML (templates.ts:69-70, 76-79) and sends them as text/html (lines 290-291). Why nothing stops it: this data comes from the remote HTTP response, not from req.query, so sanitizeMiddleware never touches it and there is no escaping or sanitization between the token endpoint response and the rendered page; the callback requires no authentication and does not verify that the caller owns the credential. Impact: stored/reflected XSS on the Flowise origin triggered by a single crafted link, running arbitrary script in the victim's browser with access to the application session and API. Fix: never render provider error text as HTML - HTML-escape error, error_description and details before interpolation (or use an auto-escaping template engine), and apply the same fix to the success page's embedded JSON.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can overwrite any user's OAuth2 credential tokens
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:157 (router.get('/callback')), which is whitelisted (packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:39) and therefore reachable by anyone, including from a cross-site /

findings.title: Unauthenticated refresh route buffers unbounded token response, OOMs server
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts:307 (POST /api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId), axios call at line 355. Attacker: an unauthenticated network caller crossing the authentication boundary — the path is whitelisted by prefix at packages/server/src/index.ts:221 against the entry '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh' in packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:40, so req.path.startsWith() matches '/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/<uuid>' and the API-key/login middleware block at index.ts:215-277 is skipped entirely; the router itself has no checkPermission/verifyToken guard. The caller needs a valid credential UUID (the same UUID is used as the OAuth state and is handed to browsers in the authorization/callback URLs and in the authorize response), after which the handler at line 309 reads credentialId, looks the credential up at line 314, decrypts it at line 325 and calls axios.post(tokenUrl, ...) at line 355. Nothing on the path stops it: no auth, no rate limiter, and axios runs with its defaults because no timeout or maxContentLength/maxBodyLength is set anywhere (no axios.defaults/axios.create override exists in the server). With timeout:0 the request hangs as long as the token endpoint stalls while holding the inbound connection; with maxContentLength:-1 and decompress:true the whole response — including gzip/br-bombed content — is inflated and buffered in memory. Because accessTokenUrl comes unvalidated from credential data, any user holding credentials:create (a non-admin, e.g. a workspace editor) can point it at their own server and make it return an endless stream or compressed bomb; the handler then spreads the unbounded object into updatedCredentialData (lines 366-370), AES-encrypts it and persists it into the credential row (lines 384-390). Impact: one tiny unauthenticated request makes the server perform an outbound TLS POST with the stored client_secret and refresh_token, an AES decrypt/encrypt and a DB write; a hostile or slow endpoint turns this into unbounded memory growth and an OOM crash of the whole Flowise instance, and the oversized blob is persisted so every later credential read decrypts and parses it (persistent amplification). Fix: remove the refresh prefix from WHITELIST_URLS or enforce verifyToken/checkPermission on this router, and set an explicit axios timeout plus maxContentLength/maxBodyLength and decompress:false (or a hard cap on the decompressed body) before spreading the provider response into the credential.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read any user record by id or email
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/user.route.ts:7 (router.get('/', userController.read)), mounted at /api/v1/user by packages/server/src/routes/index.ts:130; the path is not in WHITELIST_URLS, so the global middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285 only requires the caller to be authenticated.
Attacker: any authenticated user (a workspace member with any role, or even an API-key holder whose key belongs to another organization), crossing into other users' and other organizations' records.
The caller controls the query string; UserController.read (packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/user.controller.ts:25-37) reads query.id and query.email and calls userService.readUserById (packages/server/src/enterprise/services/user.service.ts:44-47, queryRunner.manager.findOneBy(User, { id })) or userService.readUserByEmail (lines 57-61, findOneBy(User, { email: ILike(email) })) and returns the entity after deleting only credential/tempToken/tokenExpiry (controller lines 39-44).
Nothing stops it: this route has no checkPermission/checkAnyPermission middleware at all (contrast the sibling enterprise routers such as workspace-user.route.ts, where each mutating route is gated), the controller never compares the requested id/email with req.user.id, and the service query has no organization, workspace or owner filter - the id is taken from the request and used directly. The id is validated only for UUID format (validateUserId), which does not restrict whose UUID it may be.
Impact: any authenticated principal can enumerate and read any user record on the instance by id or by email, including users of other organizations (email address, display name, status, creator ids, timestamps), giving cross-tenant PII disclosure and a reliable account-enumeration oracle.
Fix: restrict this endpoint to the caller's own record (compare req.user.id with the requested id and ignore email lookups for other users), or require a users:view permission and scope the query to the caller's organization (e.g. join OrganizationUser/WorkspaceUser and filter by req.user.activeOrganizationId) before returning the record.

findings.title: View-only member can overwrite execution records via unguarded PUT route
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/routes/executions/index.ts:11 (router.put(['/', '/:id'], executionController.updateExecution)), reachable at PUT /api/v1/executions and PUT /api/v1/executions/:id after the global authentication middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285.
Attacker: an authenticated user who lacks the executions update right - a member whose role grants only executions:view (or an API key created with the executions:view permission), crossing the role/permission boundary the application defines for execution records.
The request body and req.params.id flow into executionController.updateExecution (packages/server/src/controllers/executions/index.ts:26-35), which calls executionsService.updateExecution (packages/server/src/services/executions/index.ts:108-124); there the record is loaded with findOneBy({ id, workspaceId }) and then Object.assign(updateExecution, data) followed by merge/save writes every field present in the request body into the row.
Nothing on the path checks the caller's permission: lines 7, 8, 14 and 15 of the same router all carry checkAnyPermission('executions:view') or checkAnyPermission('executions:delete'), while this PUT route carries no middleware, and neither the controller nor the service performs any permission test or field allow-list - the body is copied wholesale. (The service does scope the lookup by req.user.activeWorkspaceId, so this is an intra-workspace privilege bypass rather than a cross-tenant one.)
Impact: a user whose role intentionally cannot modify executions can still rewrite execution records in their workspace - changing state, agentflow name/session identifiers, timestamps or any other Execution column that the permission model reserves for editors - and can mass-assign fields the update flow never intended to accept, corrupting execution history and audit data that other members rely on.
Fix: add checkAnyPermission('executions:update') to this route, and in the service copy only the whitelisted mutable fields (e.g. state, name) from the request body instead of Object.assign-ing the whole payload.

findings.title: Queue TLS certificate verification disabled, letting a MITM read Redis traffic
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/index.ts:130 (this.queueManager = QueueManager.getInstance() in queue mode)
Attacker: a network man-in-the-middle positioned between the Flowise server and its Redis (compromised host/VPC neighbour, spoofed DNS or route), crossing the boundary that the server trusts the identity of the Redis endpoint it talks to.
Path: the QueueManager constructor reads REDIS_URL and, when it starts with rediss://, assigns tlsOpts = { rejectUnauthorized: false } (lines 30-33), stores it in this.connection (lines 41-49), and setupAllQueues passes that connection object to PredictionQueue, UpsertQueue and their QueueEvents (lines 133, 144, 148; BaseQueue.ts:21-24), so every queue and queue-event connection uses TLS without certificate verification. Nothing on the path re-enables verification: the rediss:// branch hardcodes false and there is no env flag to opt back in, while the alternative REDIS_TLS branch silently accepts whatever CA is supplied.
Impact: a MITM can present a self-signed certificate, terminate the TLS session, read and modify all queue traffic (chat questions/answers, flow configurations and document payloads inside jobs), inject, retry or delete jobs, and capture the Redis AUTH password sent on the connection, which yields full access to that Redis instance.
Fix: remove rejectUnauthorized: false and keep verification on by default; let operators supply a private CA via REDIS_CA/NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, and if skipping verification is truly required make it an explicit, documented opt-in env var.

findings.title: TLS verification disabled for Redis (rejectUnauthorized: false)
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/index.ts:108 (RateLimiterManager.getInstance()) and packages/server/src/index.ts:327 (addRateLimiter for the BullMQ dashboard)
Attacker: a network man-in-the-middle on the path between the Flowise server and its Redis, crossing the boundary that the server trusts the identity of the Redis endpoint.
Path: RateLimiterManager.getConnection() (lines 58-63) checks REDIS_URL and, when it starts with rediss://, returns tls: { rejectUnauthorized: false }; that object is handed to QueueEventsProducer and QueueEvents in the constructor (lines 53-54), so those BullMQ connections negotiate TLS with no certificate validation. No later check or option re-enables verification.
Impact: a MITM can impersonate Redis, read and tamper with the rate-limit update events and the jobs in the ratelimit queue, and capture the Redis AUTH password for that connection; because these connections typically share the deployment's Redis with the session/queue data, the stolen credentials can expose far more than rate-limit counters.
Fix: delete the rejectUnauthorized: false override, verify certificates by default, and expose an explicit CA/opt-out environment variable for private-CA setups instead of disabling validation for every rediss:// URL.

findings.title: SQL injection via stored role permissions runs arbitrary SQL as DB owner
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/role.route.ts:10 (POST /api/v1/role) and :12 (PUT /api/v1/role), handled at packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/role.controller.ts:12 and :47.
Attacker: an authenticated user holding roles:manage (or an organization admin), crossing from tenant-level role management into arbitrary SQL execution as the server's database user.
Path: req.body.permissions enters RoleController.create/update, reaches RoleService.createRole (packages/server/src/enterprise/services/role.service.ts:101, which only rejects falsy values) or RoleService.updateRole (lines 127-131, no permissions check at all), and is persisted verbatim by queryRunner.manager.save into the role.permissions text column (packages/server/src/enterprise/database/migrations/postgres/1737076223692-RefactorEnterpriseDatabase.ts:95 defines it as text not null). This migration later reads every role whose permissions contain 'sso:manage' or 'apikeys:import' (lines 24-26), JSON.parses the string, filters exact matches, and JSON.stringify's the remainder (lines 31 and 36). JSON.stringify escapes double quotes but leaves single quotes untouched, and the result is concatenated directly into the UPDATE at line 37.
Why nothing stops it: no layer validates permission strings against the known permission set (only name is validated, via validateRoleName), the migration performs no parameterization, and queryRunner.query with no parameters is executed through node-postgres' simple query protocol, which accepts stacked statements, so a permissions value such as ["sso:manage","x');DROP TABLE \"user\";--"] survives parse/filter/stringify and terminates the string literal, executing the injected statement. The migration runs once on the next server start/upgrade that includes it, after the payload was planted.
Impact: the injected SQL executes with the migration's database user, typically the Flowise DB owner (superuser in common self-hosted docker-compose deployments): arbitrary DDL/DML across every organization's tables, cross-tenant data exfiltration or destruction, creation of privileged DB roles, and OS command execution via COPY ... FROM PROGRAM when the DB user is a Postgres superuser.
Fix: parameterize the statement, e.g. await queryRunner.query(`UPDATE "role" SET "permissions" = $1 WHERE "id" = $2`, [JSON.stringify(permissions), role.id]), and validate role permissions against the known permission allow-list when roles are created or updated.

findings.title: One API key dumps every tenant's chatflows via apikey route
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/controllers/chatflows/index.ts:89 (getChatflowByApiKey), registered without any auth middleware at packages/server/src/routes/chatflows/index.ts:24 and whitelisted at packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:8 ('/api/v1/chatflows/apikey/'), so the global gate in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-277 calls next() before authentication and no checkPermission runs. Attacker: an anonymous caller who holds one valid API key of their own workspace (any tenant user who can create a key, or anyone who obtained a leaked key), crossing the workspace/organization boundary into every other tenant's chatflows. Path: GET /api/v1/chatflows/apikey/<key> (no keyonly param) -> controller passes the raw path value to apikeyService.getApiKey (services/apikey/index.ts:144-157), which only checks that a row with that apiKey value exists -> chatflowsService.getChatflowByApiKey(apikey.id, req.query.keyonly) -> the QueryBuilder at lines 225-230 filters on cf.apikeyid = :apikeyid and, because keyonly is undefined, ORs in 'cf.apikeyid IS NULL' and 'cf.apikeyid = ""' -> getMany() returns whole ChatFlow entities including flowData, name and id. Nothing on the path stops it: the route is in WHITELIST_URLS so neither the JWT nor the API-key branch of the middleware executes, the service never constrains the result to the key's own workspace (the workspaceId of the matched key is loaded in validateKey.ts:26 and in the middleware but is not used here), and the only check is existence of the supplied key, which the attacker legitimately owns. Impact: one API key is enough to dump the flow definitions (node configurations, prompts, credential ids, model settings, chatflow names and ids) of every chatflow that is not bound to a flow API key across all workspaces/organizations in the deployment, and the leaked chatflow ids then feed the public endpoints /api/v1/public-chatflows/:id and /api/v1/prediction/:id. Fix: add andWhere('cf.workspaceId = :workspaceId', { workspaceId: apiKey.workspaceId }) to the query (and pass the workspaceId from the looked-up key into getChatflowByApiKey), and stop returning chatflows with no apikeyid from this public route, or restrict that fallback to the key's own workspace.

findings.title: API key list endpoint leaks other users' plaintext keys and secret hashes
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/controllers/apikey/index.ts:10 (GET /api/v1/apikey with checkPermission('apikeys:view')), which calls apikeyService.getAllApiKeys(user, page, limit). Attacker: a workspace member or an API key holding apikeys:view, crossing into the credentials of API keys created by other users of the same workspace, because the response hands back the key material itself rather than the key metadata. Path: the QueryBuilder at lines 112-119 filters only on api_key.workspaceId and calls getMany() with no select projection, so each row is a full ApiKey entity including apiKey (the plaintext secret, see database/entities/ApiKey.ts:9) and apiSecret (the scrypt hash, line 12); the permission-subset filter at lines 124-130 narrows which rows are returned but does not strip those columns, addChatflowsCount (utils/addChatflowsCount.ts) passes the objects through unchanged, and the controller returns them with res.status(200).json(apiResponse). Nothing on the path removes the secret columns, and the sibling function getAllApiKeysByOrganization at line 98 shows the intended minimal projection by selecting only api_key.keyName and api_key.permissions. Impact: every caller with apikeys:view receives the plaintext API keys and secret hashes of all other keys in the workspace whose permissions are a subset of their own, and a key value is directly usable as a Bearer token on the API-key routes (index.ts:239-276) and on the public flow routes, so a view-only caller ends up holding usable credentials that were issued to other users. Fix: project only the fields the UI needs (id, keyName, permissions, workspaceId, updatedDate) in the query and never return apiKey or apiSecret from a list endpoint; return the generated key value once from the createApiKey response and keep it out of subsequent reads.

findings.title: Org admin injects SQL through unescaped role permissions in migration
findings.description: Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/role.route.ts:12 (and :10) — POST/PUT /api/v1/role, guarded only by checkPermission('roles:manage'), which packages/server/src/enterprise/rbac/PermissionCheck.ts:10-12 passes unconditionally for any organization admin. Attacker: an authenticated organization admin (a tenant user the app does not trust with the shared database), crossing the tenant boundary into arbitrary SQL execution against the Flowise database. The path: req.body.permissions is passed by RoleController.create/update (packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/role.controller.ts:12,47) to RoleService.createRole/updateRole (packages/server/src/enterprise/services/role.service.ts:92-144), which store it in the role.permissions text column with no validation (createRole checks only truthiness; updateRole does not inspect permissions at all), and there is no body schema validation on the route. On the next server start (packages/server/src/index.ts:87 runMigrations), this migration selects role rows whose permissions contain sso:manage/apikeys:import (line 25, constant operands), JSON.parses the stored string (line 31), filters it, and interpolates JSON.stringify(permissions) and role.id directly into the UPDATE at line 37. JSON.stringify does not escape single quotes, so a stored permission such as x' WHERE id='<victim>' -- terminates the SQL string literal and rewrites the statement; nothing on the path escapes, parameterizes or allow-lists the value. Impact: at the next upgrade/restart the attacker's SQL runs as the Flowise database user — in PostgreSQL stacked statements execute, so an org admin can read or modify other tenants' users, credentials, API keys and roles, grant themselves sso:manage/roles:manage, or copy sensitive rows into records they can read back through the API. Fix: parameterize the migration (e.g. queryRunner.query('UPDATE "role" SET "permissions" = ? WHERE "id" = ?', [JSON.stringify(permissions), role.id]), using $1-style placeholders per driver) or use the repository/query builder, and validate permissions against the Permissions allow-list in RoleService.createRole/updateRole before persisting; the same unparameterized interpolation exists in the postgres, mysql and mariadb copies of this migration and needs the same fix.

findings.title: Unauthenticated attacker can register as OWNER of any existing organization
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/account.route.ts:9 (router.post('/register', accountController.register), reachable unauthenticated because /api/v1/account/register is in WHITELIST_URLS).
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller crossing the tenant boundary by joining an existing organization they do not belong to as its OWNER.
The body is passed untouched from account.controller.ts:10 into AccountService.register -> saveRegisterAccount -> createRegisterAccount. In the Platform.CLOUD branch, data.organization comes straight from req.body (initializeAccountDTO only defaults it to {}), and line 223 only creates a new organization when data.organization.id is falsy. If the caller supplies organization: { id: <victim org id> } the creation is skipped, data.organizationUser.organizationId is set to that caller-supplied id (line 227), data.organizationUser.role is set to the general OWNER role (line 162) and the row is created with it (line 230), then the organization is persisted with the caller-supplied primary key (line 254, OrganizationService.saveOrganization -> manager.save), overwriting the victim organization's name/customerId/subscriptionId with the attacker's new Stripe customer.
Nothing on the path checks that organization.id belongs to the caller or that the caller may join it: register has no authentication and no ownership check, and the OrganizationUser service merely creates the row with the role it was given. The OrganizationUser/WorkspaceUser rows make the attacker an organization admin on next login (isOrganizationAdmin is derived from workspaceUser.roleId === general OWNER role in middleware/passport/index.ts:178), giving full read/write access to the victim tenant's workspaces, chatflows and credentials, plus destruction of the victim's billing linkage.
Fix: never accept organization.id/workspace.id/role from the registration body - always create the organization/workspace server-side and look up roles by the created organization, or require an authenticated invite/admin flow for joining an existing organization.

findings.title: Cross-tenant invite lets any user join another tenant's workspace and org
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/account.route.ts:12-17 (router.post('/invite', ... checkAnyPermission('workspace:add-user,users:manage'), accountController.invite)); controller at packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/account.controller.ts:20.
Attacker: an authenticated user who holds workspace:add-user or users:manage in their own tenant, crossing into another tenant's workspace and organization.
The handler saveInviteAccount reads the target workspace with data.workspace.id straight from the request body (line 290), then uses that workspace's organizationId to resolve the role (line 297) and to create OrganizationUser/WorkspaceUser rows in that organization (lines 320-335, roleId taken from data.role.id). The only guard is checkAnyPermission (PermissionCheck.ts:24), which checks the permission strings carried in the caller's own JWT/permissions - it never compares the requested workspace/organization with req.user.activeOrganizationId, and nothing in the service verifies membership either. Because the role lookup is scoped to the victim workspace's organization, the caller can pick any role of the victim tenant (including a full-permission custom role) and invite an email they control.
Impact: a user who is only a workspace admin/member in tenant A can add themselves (or anyone) to any workspace of tenant B, and once they accept the invite and log in they get the victim workspace's chatflows, credentials and data - a full cross-tenant access-control bypass.
Fix: resolve the workspace through the caller's active organization (e.g. readWorkspaceByOrganizationId(req.user.activeOrganizationId)) and reject when data.workspace.id is not in that organization; scope the role lookup to the same organization.

findings.title: Unauthenticated reset-password bypass lets anyone take over any account
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/account.route.ts:29 (router.post('/reset-password', accountController.resetPassword)); the path is in WHITELIST_URLS at packages/server/src/utils/constants.ts:34, so the /api/v1 gate in packages/server/src/index.ts:215-285 calls next() without a session, API key or x-request-from header.
Attacker: an unauthenticated caller on the network who knows or guesses a user's e-mail address, crossing into another user's account (including the deployment owner) and gaining full control of it.
Path: req.body -> AccountController.resetPassword (packages/server/src/enterprise/controllers/account.controller.ts:67-75, body passed through untouched) -> AccountService.resetPassword -> readUserByEmail (user.service.ts:57-61) -> the only gates are line 570 (`if (user.tempToken !== data.user.tempToken)`) and lines 573-579 (expiry), then lines 582-597 hash and store the attacker-supplied `user.password` and call destroyAllSessionsForUser.
Why nothing stops it: the comparison is an equality test against a column that is NULL for a freshly registered OPEN_SOURCE owner (account.service.ts:123-131 never sets tempToken; user.entity.ts:30-34 declares tempToken/tokenExpiry nullable), so a body of {"user":{"email":"owner@victim","tempToken":null,"password":"NewPass123!"}} makes `null !== null` false and passes; for any account that has verified its e-mail or changed its password the column is '' (account.service.ts:517, user.service.ts:174) so `"tempToken":""` passes as well. The expiry gate cannot stop it either: tokenExpiry is NULL/undefined for those same accounts, moment(null) is an Invalid Date and moment(undefined) is 'now', so now.diff(...) is NaN or 0 and `Math.abs(diff) > 15` is false. There is no reset-token validation, no single-use/consumption check tied to an e-mail-delivered secret, no rate limiting, and no authentication on the route.
Impact: any unauthenticated attacker can set the password of any account whose e-mail they know (the login and forgot-password responses also distinguish USER_NOT_FOUND from other errors, making e-mail enumeration trivial) and then log in as that user; because resetPassword calls destroyAllSessionsForUser, the legitimate owner is also logged out, so the takeover is silent and complete, including owner/admin rights over the whole deployment.
Fix: require a server-generated, non-empty, single-use reset token: reject the request when `!data.user.tempToken` or `!user.tempToken`, compare the stored value with a constant-time comparison, store only a hash of the token with an explicit expiry column, invalidate it on use, and rate-limit /forgot-password and /reset-password. Also return a generic success response from forgot-password/resend-verification so e-mail addresses cannot be enumerated.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can change another tenant's Stripe subscription plan
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:23 (POST /api/v1/organization/update-subscription-plan) -> OrganizationController.updateSubscriptionPlan at organization.controller.ts:149.
Attacker: any authenticated user of any organization (including a workspace API-key holder with no organization-admin rights), crossing the tenant boundary into another organization's paid Stripe subscription.
Path: req.body.subscriptionId is taken at controller line 151 and passed unchecked to identityManager.updateSubscriptionPlan(req, subscriptionId, newPlanId, prorationDate) at line 162; IdentityManager.updateSubscriptionPlan (IdentityManager.ts:373-382) only checks that subscriptionId is truthy and that req.user exists, then calls stripeManager.updateSubscriptionPlan (StripeManager.ts:501) which mutates the Stripe subscription and rewrites the cached plan features/quotas for that subscription.
Why nothing stops it: the router file mounts no checkPermission or checkFeatureByPlan (unlike organization-user.route.ts:11-15 or workspace.route.ts:9-22), and IdentityManager never compares subscriptionId with req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId - the only barrier in the whole path is 'is the caller logged in'.
Impact: any low-privileged user or integration API key can change the paid plan (upgrade/downgrade) of any other tenant's Stripe subscription, causing unwanted charges on the victim's payment method or stripping the victim's plan features; subscription ids are guessable/obtainable through the GET /organization endpoint which leaks them.
Fix: in the controller or IdentityManager, reject the call unless subscriptionId equals req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId (or the caller is an organization admin of the organization that owns it), and add a checkPermission/admin guard to the route.

findings.title: Authenticated user can overwrite any tenant's organization via PUT body mass assignment
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:11 (PUT /api/v1/organization) -> OrganizationController.update at organization.controller.ts:49, which passes req.body straight through at line 52.
Attacker: any authenticated user of any organization (any role, or a workspace API key) crossing into another tenant's organization record.
Path: req.body.id selects the organization loaded by readOrganizationById at organization.service.ts:98; line 100 only verifies that body.updatedBy names an existing user (any user id works, including the attacker's own); line 105 forces createdBy back to the old value, but line 107 merges the entire remaining body into the loaded entity (queryRunner.manager.merge) and line 110 saves it, so every body field - name, subscriptionId, customerId, updatedBy - is persisted.
Why nothing stops it: there is no check that the target organization id equals req.user.activeOrganizationId, no membership lookup in OrganizationUser, no role check, and the route has no middleware guard; the id comes from the request body and only needs to be a valid UUID.
Impact: cross-tenant mass assignment - the attacker can rename a victim organization and, more seriously, rewrite its subscriptionId/customerId Stripe identifiers (for example repoint their own organization at a victim's paid subscription to inherit its features/quotas, or repoint a victim organization at the attacker's data), and forge updatedBy.
Fix: require body.id to equal req.user.activeOrganizationId and restrict the updatable field list to non-privileged fields such as name (drop subscriptionId/customerId from client input), plus add an organization-admin permission guard on the route.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can change another tenant's subscription seat count
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:19 (POST /api/v1/organization/update-additional-seats) -> OrganizationController.updateAdditionalSeats at organization.controller.ts:128.
Attacker: any authenticated user of any organization (including a restricted workspace API key), crossing the tenant boundary into another organization's billing.
Path: req.body.subscriptionId/quantity/prorationDate are read at controller lines 130-139 and passed at line 141 to identityManager.updateAdditionalSeats(subscriptionId, quantity, prorationDate); IdentityManager.ts:323-329 only checks that subscriptionId is truthy and then calls StripeManager.updateAdditionalSeats (StripeManager.ts:365-427), which updates the subscription's seat item, immediately invoices it (proration_behavior: 'always_invoice') and even pays the generated invoice at line 414.
Why nothing stops it: no comparison against req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId, no route guard, no tenant scoping anywhere on the path.
Impact: an attacker can set an arbitrary seat quantity on any other tenant's subscription, forcing immediate invoices and charges on the victim's stored payment method (or failing payments), and corrupting that subscription's cached quotas via the usage cache update in IdentityManager.ts:351-359.
Fix: use req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId instead of the client-supplied id (or verify equality before acting), and add an organization-admin permission guard to the route.

findings.title: Authenticated user can read any tenant's organization by id or name
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:7 (GET /api/v1/organization?id=... or ?name=...) -> OrganizationController.read at organization.controller.ts:22.
Attacker: any authenticated user of any organization (any role, or a workspace API key), crossing into another tenant's organization record.
Path: req.query.id is passed at line 32 to OrganizationService.readOrganizationById (organization.service.ts:35-38, an unscoped findOneBy(Organization, { id })), or req.query.name at line 35 to readOrganizationByName (organization.service.ts:47-50, findOneBy name); the full entity is serialized back at line 41.
Why nothing stops it: neither lookup is filtered by the caller's organization, no check that query.id === req.user.activeOrganizationId exists, and this router has no guard at all (the read endpoint has no checkPermission in any layer).
Impact: cross-tenant data disclosure of another organization's id, name, customerId and subscriptionId; the name-based lookup also allows enumerating organizations by name, and the leaked Stripe subscriptionId/customerId are the exact inputs the sibling billing endpoints (update-subscription-plan, update-additional-seats, customer-default-source) accept without ownership checks, so this is the reconnaissance step of a billing-takeover chain.
Fix: ignore client-supplied id/name and scope the lookup to req.user.activeOrganizationId, or require organization-admin permission for arbitrary lookups.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another tenant's Stripe billing profile
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:15 (GET /api/v1/organization/customer-default-source?customerId=...) -> OrganizationController.getCustomerWithDefaultSource at organization.controller.ts:77.
Attacker: any authenticated user of any organization (any role, or a workspace API key), crossing into another customer's Stripe billing profile.
Path: req.query.customerId is read at line 79 and passed at line 84 to identityManager.getCustomerWithDefaultSource (IdentityManager.ts:307-313), which calls StripeManager.getCustomerWithDefaultSource (StripeManager.ts:256-271) and retrieves the customer with default_source and invoice_settings.default_payment_method expanded, returning the whole Stripe customer object.
Why nothing stops it: the handler never compares customerId with req.user.activeOrganizationCustomerId, the router mounts no permission middleware, and Stripe will happily return any customer id to the server's secret key.
Impact: disclosure of any customer's payment-method details, billing address/email and balance (payment instrument metadata), which combined with the unauthenticated-by-tenant GET /organization lookup of customerId gives a full cross-tenant billing-profile read; the sibling GET /organization/plan-proration and /additional-seats-proration have the same flaw and leak credit balances and invoice totals for arbitrary subscriptionIds.
Fix: derive customerId from req.user.activeOrganizationCustomerId and ignore the query parameter, and add an organization-admin permission guard to the route.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can self-create an organization and become OWNER
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:9 (POST /api/v1/organization) -> OrganizationController.create at organization.controller.ts:12, which passes req.body directly at line 15.
Attacker: any authenticated user, including one with no users:manage permission and a chat-only workspace API key, gaining organization-owner power and attaching an arbitrary paid subscription.
Path: req.body (name, createdBy, and any other Organization column such as subscriptionId/customerId) flows into OrganizationUserService.createOrganization (organization-user.service.ts:245): line 249 only checks that body.createdBy is an existing user id (the attacker's own id works), line 252 creates the organization from the raw body via OrganizationService.createNewOrganization (organization.service.ts:60-66, which writes the body fields onto the entity), and lines 254-262 then look up the general OWNER role and insert an OrganizationUser row making the body.createdBy user the owner of the new organization.
Why nothing stops it: the route has no checkPermission/checkFeatureByPlan guard, and the service validates nothing except user existence - neither who may create an organization nor which fields may be set.
Impact: self-service privilege escalation - a plain user or restricted API key becomes OWNER (isOrganizationAdmin true, full permissions) of a new tenant without any invite/role flow - and mass assignment of subscriptionId/customerId lets the new organization be pointed at a subscription the attacker does not own, inheriting its paid features and quotas (the subscription id can be harvested through the unguarded GET /organization endpoint).
Fix: set createdBy from req.user.id instead of the body, require an explicit organization-creation permission/plan check on the route, and allow-list the accepted fields (name only).

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read other tenants' billing proration data
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:21 (GET /api/v1/organization/plan-proration?subscriptionId=...&newPlanId=...) -> OrganizationController.getPlanProration at organization.controller.ts:110.
Attacker: any authenticated user of any organization (any role, or a workspace API key), crossing into another tenant's billing data.
Path: req.query.subscriptionId/newPlanId are read at lines 112-118 and passed at line 120 to identityManager.getPlanProration (IdentityManager.ts:364-371), which calls StripeManager.getPlanProration (StripeManager.ts:429-...), retrieving the subscription, the customer's credit balance and proration amounts.
Why nothing stops it: no check that subscriptionId matches req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId, and the route carries no permission guard.
Impact: financial reconnaissance of any tenant's subscription - plan changes, credit balance, upcoming invoice totals and pricing - using ids leaked by the unguarded GET /organization endpoint.
Fix: ignore the client-supplied subscriptionId and use req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId, and add an organization-admin permission guard to the route.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can read another tenant's billing/proration data by subscriptionId
findings.description:
Entry: packages/server/src/enterprise/routes/organization.route.ts:17 (GET /api/v1/organization/additional-seats-proration?subscriptionId=...&quantity=...) -> OrganizationController.getAdditionalSeatsProration at organization.controller.ts:92.
Attacker: any authenticated user of any organization (any role, or a workspace API key), crossing into another tenant's billing data.
Path: req.query.subscriptionId and quantity are read at lines 94-100 and passed at line 102 to identityManager.getAdditionalSeatsProration (IdentityManager.ts:315-321), which calls StripeManager.getAdditionalSeatsProration (StripeManager.ts:273-362), retrieving the subscription, the customer's credit balance, the upcoming invoice and the proration amount.
Why nothing stops it: the handler never compares subscriptionId with req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId and the router mounts no permission middleware.
Impact: disclosure of another tenant's credit balance, invoice totals and seat proration amounts for any subscription id (harvestable via the unguarded GET /organization read).
Fix: use req.user.activeOrganizationSubscriptionId instead of the query parameter and add an organization-admin permission guard to the route.
